headline: Can You Maximize Your Own Coolness?

paragraphs.text: For centuries, aura was understood to be a gift from the gods—an ineffable trait bestowed on special beings. Think of Venus in Botticelli’s 15th-century painting, looking bored yet fabulous as she floats to shore. (As it happens, in that painting, both a god and a nymph named Aura gaze lovingly at Venus.) But now the word is being used more liberally to describe suave celebrities, anime characters, and everyday cool kids alike. It has also gained a new meaning—perhaps most clearly demonstrated by the rise of the phrase aura farming, which evokes hard work rather than divinely granted cool.

Aura farming pulls from gaming-world slang that suggests that people are putting in the effort to level up. (See also: aura level and aura points.) Although aura farming has been around for a bit, its usage was inadvertently boosted last year by Rayyan Arkan Dikha, a young Indonesian boy who went viral for dancing effortlessly on the bow of a fast-moving racing boat, and whose admirers helped popularize the phrase. Soon after, it took off. The concept has since spawned real-life “aura battles,” in which participants invoke jokes, dances, and internet references to prove their greatness. Recently, South Park even released an episode satirizing aura battles; at one point, a character hits his face with a hammer (a clear reference to looksmaxxing) in hopes of chiseling his jawline enough to beat his opponent.

Last year, Oxford University Press shortlisted aura farming for its Word of the Year pick, defining it as “the cultivation of an impressive, attractive, or charismatic persona.” As the publisher jokingly explained in a social-media campaign, an aura farmer might drink matcha, wear wired headphones, and kindly inform you that they went on a date with Luca Guadagnino’s director of photography. In other words, aura farming and its variants reveal a very modern understanding of what it is to be cool: Nowadays, coolness isn’t just God-given—You either got it or you don’t, honey! It’s also seen as something that can, and should, be meticulously optimized.

For most of human history, cultures and religions around the world depicted auras via symbols reserved for divine figures, such as deities. Think of the halos used in Buddhist iconography or the billowing garments used in Greco-Roman art. But over time, auras started to be visualized in art more widely. When the first halo appeared in Christian art, in the fourth century C.E., it was reserved for members of the Holy Trinity, Jeremy Stolow, a communications professor at Concordia University, writes in Picturing Aura. But eventually, he notes, halos were used to denote the sanctity of people “across the Christian pantheon,” including saints, popes, prophets, and disciples.

In the late 1800s, scientific breakthroughs shifted how people understood energy and life on Earth, and the concept of auras was further democratized. People began to think “that everybody has an aura, and maybe even not just humans,” Stolow told me—other animals and plants might, too. Discoveries such as the X-ray underscored the notion that invisible things could be made visible, and spiritual groups such as the Theosophists (predecessors of the New Age movement) led a surging interest in energy fields, auras, and clairvoyance. Auras, to some, started to be seen as a legitimate phenomenon for scientific study. Perhaps they were a natural force, like molecules and atoms, that some new gadget would one day lay bare to the naked eye. Throughout the 20th century, Stolow said, use of the word aura skyrocketed as people employed it to describe a kind of subtle emanation.

It’s a nice idea: aura as a secret ingredient of the universe. But these days, the word has evolved into a synonym for swagger. Phoebe Nicholson, an executive editor at Oxford University Press who helped pick the Word of the Year, described how aura’s modern meaning undercuts similar terms, such as X-factor, it girl, and star. Those words arose largely during the golden age of Hollywood in the mid-20th century, when celebrity was typically viewed from a distance, through a lens of “otherworldliness,” she told me, and people were “but peasants looking at it.” Aura farming, though, places coolness within reach: It suggests that although no one is born wearing rhinestones, anyone can put them on and dazzle.

This focus on persona building seems to be a symptom of the broader self-improvement ethos that’s common today. Just as faces and bodies can be tweaked, people’s “subtle emanations” can supposedly be boosted as well. A whole genre of videos has popped up online dispensing advice on how to refine one’s aura. Tips include wearing linen, changing your posture and gait, using a signature scent, and—of course—buying an electrolyte product strategically placed in a video’s corner. Some aura farmers might even shell out $34 a month for an app that promises to help “start upgrading your character” to one with a better mind and soul.

Crucially, this trend of aura enhancement is framed not just in gamified lingo but in economic terms, too. “It’s phrased in this very capitalist language of accumulation,” Stolow said: “I get points; I expend them; I lose them; I invest.” In this way, aura resembles the term identity capital, a concept that sees hobbies, test scores, fashion, and life experiences as wealth-building projects that can be traded in the marketplace of adulthood. Similarly, aura points might be cashed in for attention, renown, a brand deal, a lover.

The catch is that aura levels are subject to the fickle opinions of other people. And delivered in a certain tone, aura farming can be a pejorative—used to cut down those who are trying too hard. One YouTube compilation of “Aura Farming Fails,” for instance, shows a man flexing his muscles in front of a bathroom mirror before accidentally knocking down a soap dispenser.

Here, the bestowers of aura are not gods but social-media commenters: “The role of the spectator is essential,” Stolow noted, “to the whole functioning of this aura economy.” Cultivating aura becomes, for some, a part of online life. But if you botch the attempt or your efforts are too obvious, a jury of your peers can decide that your shine is gone. The fear of losing this quality is, naturally, what drives the demand for all of the products that claim to boost it. “I think we should stop rating looks and coolness,” one character shrewdly concludes near the end of that South Park episode, “so that companies stop preying on people’s insecurities.”

Reading too much into a phrase that’s largely used for fun can, of course, be futile. And people judged others’ attempts at coolness long before the Internet Age. Still, applying video-game language and points systems to real life can cause problems, Adam Aleksic, the author of Algospeak, told me: “We start framing our interactions in these terms.” Put too much stock in your aura level, and you might start seeing your own human value—and that of others—as changeable, rather than inherent. Most of us will never be cool in that effortless Venus way, but mere mortals were never meant to be.
